Unit 8: Period 8 (1945–1980)

📋 Everything from Unit 8 in one place — 15 topics from the Cold War through Watergate. Use the animation to lock in the 1960s Civil Rights Movement before your test.
8.1

Contextualizing Period 8

  • U.S. emerges from WWII as the dominant power, immediately in Cold War rivalry with the USSR.
  • Postwar boom, the Civil Rights Movement, and Vietnam/Watergate reshape American life and trust in government.
Cold War
Period 8 at a glance.
8.2

The Cold War from 1945 to 1980

  • Containment: prevent the spread of communism (Korea, later Vietnam).
  • Cuban Missile Crisis (1962): closest the world came to nuclear war.
  • Détente (Nixon, 1970s): eases tensions with the USSR.
ContainmentCuban Missile Crisis
The Cold War, 1945–1980.
8.3

The Red Scare

  • HUAC investigates alleged communist influence, especially in Hollywood.
  • McCarthyism: sweeping, often unsubstantiated accusations of communist sympathy.
HUACMcCarthyism
The Red Scare & McCarthyism.
8.4

Economy after 1945

  • GI Bill: veterans' education benefits + low-cost home loans → fuels suburbanization.
  • Interstate Highway System connects growing suburbs.
GI BillSuburbanization
The postwar economic boom.
8.5

Culture after 1945

  • Television creates shared national culture; Baby Boom reshapes demographics.
  • Beat Generation rejects conformity — foreshadows 1960s counterculture.
Baby boomBeat Generation
Postwar American culture.
8.6

Early Steps in the Civil Rights Movement

  • Brown v. Board (1954): segregated schools unconstitutional.
  • Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–56): sparked by Rosa Parks, brings MLK to prominence.
  • Little Rock Crisis (1957): federal troops enforce integration.
Brown v. BoardMontgomery Bus Boycott
Early civil rights milestones.
8.7

America as a World Power

  • Marshall Plan: rebuilds Western Europe, also contains communism.
  • NATO (1949): first permanent peacetime military alliance.
Marshall PlanNATO
America's postwar global role.
8.8

The Vietnam War

  • Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964): broad war-making authority for Johnson.
  • Tet Offensive (1968): military setback for North Vietnam, but shocks U.S. public opinion & erodes support.
  • Paris Peace Accords (1973) → Saigon falls (1975).
Gulf of Tonkin ResolutionTet Offensive
Trap: Tet was a military defeat for North Vietnam but a public-opinion turning point against the war — know both sides.
The Vietnam War.
8.9

The Great Society

  • Medicare/Medicaid: health coverage for elderly/poor. War on Poverty: Head Start, food stamps.
  • Immigration Act of 1965: ends national-origin quotas.
Great SocietyMedicare and Medicaid
LBJ's Great Society programs.
8.10

The African American Civil Rights Movement (1960s)

  • Sit-in movement (1960) → March on Washington (1963, “I Have a Dream”) → Civil Rights Act (1964) → Voting Rights Act (1965).
  • MLK assassinated (1968).
March on WashingtonVoting Rights Act
The Civil Rights Movement, 1960s.

8.11

The Civil Rights Movement Expands

  • Early movement: nonviolent, integrationist (MLK, SCLC).
  • Later movements: more militant (Black Panthers); inspires Chicano movement, AIM, women's rights.
Black PanthersAmerican Indian Movement
The movement expands & diversifies.
8.12

Youth Culture of the 1960s and 1970s

  • Counterculture rejects mainstream values; closely tied to the antiwar movement.
  • Rock music becomes the soundtrack of youth identity; widens the generation gap.
CountercultureGeneration gap
Youth culture, 1960s–70s.
8.13

The Environment and Natural Resources

  • Silent Spring (1962) launches the environmental movement.
  • First Earth Day (1970) → EPA created (1970).
  • 1970s energy crisis links environmental & foreign policy.
Silent SpringEPA
The rise of environmentalism.
8.14

Society in Transition

  • Watergate + stagflation badly damage trust in active, liberal government.
  • Rising New Right conservative movement gains strength through the 1970s.
WatergateStagflation
Liberalism vs. a rising right.
8.15

Continuity and Change in Period 8

  • Change: legal segregation ends; federal domestic role expands (Great Society).
  • Continuity: racial inequality persists in practice; U.S. remains a global superpower throughout.
Continuity and change
1945 vs. 1980.
★

Master Summary Table

EventKey Fact
Brown v. Board (1954)Overturns “separate but equal,” provides legal momentum for the movement
Civil Rights Act (1964)Bans discrimination in public accommodations & employment
Voting Rights Act (1965)Bans discriminatory voting practices like literacy tests
Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964)Grants Johnson broad authority to escalate Vietnam without a war declaration
WatergateNixon's abuse of power + cover-up; devastates trust in government
⚠

Commonly Missed on the Exam

  • Containment justified both Korea AND Vietnam — know it's the same underlying policy applied twice.
  • The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) is the closest the Cold War came to actual nuclear war — distinct from the Berlin Wall or Korea.
  • Brown v. Board (1954) ended legal school segregation, but did not itself desegregate schools in practice — that took years of further action.
  • The Great Society (Medicare, War on Poverty) expanded federal power further than even the New Deal.
  • Watergate and stagflation are two separate causes of declining trust — one political, one economic.
  • Later civil rights groups (Black Panthers) didn't replace early nonviolent activism — both existed simultaneously with different strategies.
